title: Figures, axes and lines
objectives: Make a line chart with matplotlib’s figure and axes objects.
Name the parts of a chart and the object that owns each one.

screens.question: What does each point on the line stand for?

options.text: One pair: a day from `days` and the close at the same position in `closes`
One close; matplotlib spaces the closes out by itself

screens.title: Figure and axes
screens.prose:
The chart came from this code.

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(days, closes)
ax.set_title("Harbour closes")
```

`plt.subplots()` returns two objects: the **figure** `fig` and the **axes** `ax`.
screens.question: Match each object to the part of the chart it is.

slots.label: The whole image: everything that gets saved
The plotting area, with its ticks and axis labels
The line through the ten closes
The words above the plotting area

hints.text: Start with the biggest part: which object holds everything else?
`ax.plot` puts a line inside the axes, so the line belongs to `ax`.
The figure is the whole image. The axes is the plotting box. The line lives in `ax.lines`, and the title is `ax.title`.

feedback.correct: The figure holds the axes, and the axes holds the line and the title.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work from the outside in: image, plotting box, line, title.

byKey.t-fig: The figure is the whole image. It holds the axes, and it is what gets saved.
byKey.t-ax: `ax` is the plotting box: the ticks, the axis labels and the data inside. The figure is the image around it.
byKey.t-line: `ax.plot` added one line to the list `ax.lines`. The first line is `ax.lines[0]`.
byKey.t-title: `ax.title` is the text above the plotting box. `ax.set_title` fills it in.

explain.text: The figure is the outer container you save. The axes is one plotting area inside it, and it owns everything drawn there. That is why the drawing calls are methods of `ax`.

widget.solution:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def plot_closes(days, closes):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    # draw the closes against the days on ax
    ax.plot(days, closes)
    return ax

screens.title: Two figures, one plt.plot
screens.prose:
`plt.plot` also draws a line, but you do not say where.

```python
fig1, ax1 = plt.subplots()
fig2, ax2 = plt.subplots()
plt.plot(days, closes)
print(len(ax1.lines), len(ax2.lines))
```

state.caption: One `plt.plot` call drew this line. On which axes?

screens.question: What does it print?

options.why: You expected `plt.plot` to use the first axes. It uses the current axes, the one made last.
One call draws one line. `plt.plot` does not copy it onto every axes.

options.text: An error: `plt.plot` needs to be told the axes
options.why: `plt.plot` finds the current axes itself. It never asks which one you meant.

hints.text: Which axes did matplotlib make most recently?
`plt.plot` draws on the current axes, which `plt.gca()` returns.
The current axes is `ax2`, made by the second `plt.subplots()`. So `ax1` has 0 lines and `ax2` has 1.

feedback.correct: `plt.plot` went to `ax2`, the axes made last.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. `plt.plot` draws on the current axes: the one made most recently.

byKey.first: You expected the first axes. `plt.plot` used the current one, `ax2`, made by the second `plt.subplots()`.

explain.text: `plt.plot` picks the current axes for you, here `ax2`. With several charts open, that guess goes wrong without a word. `ax1.plot(days, closes)` says exactly where the line goes, so we use `ax` from the start.

screens.title: Plot twice
screens.prose:
A notebook cell runs twice by accident, and both runs draw on the same `ax`.

```python
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(days, closes)
ax.plot(days, closes)
```

The chart still looks like one line.
screens.question: What is `len(ax.lines)`?

widget.label: Number of lines
widget.accept: 2: each call to `ax.plot` adds a line.

hints.text: Each call to `ax.plot` adds a line. Does a second call replace the first?
Two identical lines are drawn on the same pixels.
Two calls, two lines: `len(ax.lines)` is 2.

feedback.correct: Two calls, two lines, drawn on the same pixels.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the calls to `ax.plot`.

byKey.one: You trusted the picture. The second line sits exactly on the first, so you cannot see it, but `ax.lines` holds both.
byKey.zero: Both calls drew. `ax.lines` lists every line on the axes.

explain.text: `ax.plot` always adds and never replaces, so `len(ax.lines)` is 2. The second line hides the first exactly, so the picture cannot tell you. That is why the tests count `ax.lines` instead of looking.

screens.title: Mixing the two styles
screens.prose:
A colleague mixes `plt` habits with the axes object.

```python
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(days, closes)
ax.xlabel("Day")
```
screens.question: What happens on the last line?

options.text: The x axis is labelled Day
options.why: You carried `plt.xlabel` over to `ax`. On an axes the method is `ax.set_xlabel`.

options.text: It stops: `AttributeError: 'Axes' object has no attribute 'xlabel'`
It returns the current label, which is empty
options.why: That is `ax.get_xlabel()`. `ax.xlabel` does not exist, so Python stops.

options.text: Every axes in the figure is labelled Day
options.why: No call labels every axes at once, and `ax.xlabel` is not a method at all.

hints.text: The `plt` functions and the `ax` methods have different names.
On an axes, a method that sets something starts with `set_`.
`ax` has `set_xlabel`, not `xlabel`, so Python raises an `AttributeError`.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check whether an `Axes` object has a method called `xlabel`.

byKey.works: You carried `plt.xlabel` over to `ax`. Axes methods that change something start with `set_`: `ax.set_xlabel("Day")`.
byKey.get: Reading the label is `ax.get_xlabel()`. Plain `ax.xlabel` is not there, so Python stops.

explain.text:
`plt.xlabel` and `ax.set_xlabel` do the same job in the two styles. Mixing them fails loudly here. `ax.title("...")` fails too, because `ax.title` is the title's text object.

```python
ax.xlabel("Day")      # AttributeError
ax.set_xlabel("Day")  # works
```

screens.title: The pattern
screens.prose:
Every chart in this course follows the same shape.

```python
fig, ax = plt.subplots()   # a figure holding one axes
ax.plot(x, y)              # a line on that axes
ax.set_title("...")        # set_ methods change the axes
ax.set_xlabel("...")
fig.savefig("chart.png")   # the figure is what you save
```
screens.question: You want the chart in a file. Which line does it?

options.text: `fig.savefig("chart.png")`
`ax.savefig("chart.png")`
options.why: You asked the axes to save. Only the figure is the whole image, so `Axes` has no `savefig`.

options.text: `plt.show()`
options.why: `plt.show()` opens a window to look at the chart. It writes no file, and a server has no window.

feedback.correct: The figure is the whole image, so the figure saves it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which object is the whole image?

explain.text: `fig.savefig("chart.png")` writes the whole figure, axes and all. Call it after drawing, or the file holds an empty chart.

screens.title: In what order?
screens.prose: A script must make the axes before it draws, and draw before it saves.
screens.question: Put the lines in an order that saves a chart of the closes.

hints.text: What must exist before `ax.plot` can run?
`ax` comes from `plt.subplots()`, which needs `plt` imported first.
Import, make the figure and axes, draw, then save.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each line needs something an earlier line made.

explain.text: `plt` must be imported before `plt.subplots()` can make `fig` and `ax`. Saving last captures the line. Save before `ax.plot` and the file holds an empty chart.

screens.title: Save a backtest's equity curve
screens.prose: A backtest gives the daily value of a £100,000 portfolio. The morning report needs its equity curve as an image file, titled `Equity curve`.
screens.question: Complete `save_equity`: plot `values` against `days`, set the title, save the figure to `path` and return `ax`.

widget.starter:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def save_equity(days, values, path):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    ...
    return ax
widget.solution:
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def save_equity(days, values, path):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    ax.plot(days, values)
    ax.set_title("Equity curve")
    fig.savefig(path)
    return ax

explain.text: The y axis belongs to `ax`, and axes setters start with `set_`. So it is `ax.set_ylabel("Close (£)")`, and `ax.get_ylabel()` reads it back.
